title: A 50-Year-Old Frog Mystery Points to a Fungus
paragraphs: For about fifty years, scientists did not know why frogs in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest began to vanish in the 1970s and 1980s. A new study in the journal Molecular Ecology now points to a fungus called chytrid, which can seriously harm amphibians.

The team, led by Jack Boyette of the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute and Penn State, tested hundreds of preserved frogs from the Boracéia Biological Station in São Paulo. The animals were collected by researcher Ronald Heyer during expeditions in the 1970s and 1980s. No frog collected before 1979 carried the fungus, but more than half of those collected in the 1980s did. The worst declines happened between 1979 and 1982.

Visits to the same area between 2022 and 2024 found twelve of the seventeen species, so many populations seem to have recovered, even though the fungus is still present. The authors suggest that some frogs may have become more tolerant of it over time. This is only an idea, and five species were not found, so their fate is unknown. Because the study covers one site, it cannot explain every decline in the region.
